turns.t: Good morning, Singapore — it's Monday, the thirty-first of August. This is The Meridian Briefing.
Twelve desks. One world. Twenty minutes — let's go. [excited]
Three to start. An island of four hundred thousand people looked Europe in the eye and said, no thank you.
Nvidia reaches for the open-source town square and offers to buy the whole thing.
And in China, the machine grew a plush body. [wry] We'll get there.
[chuckles] We are absolutely getting there. Start me on the island.
Iceland. On Saturday they held a referendum — not on joining the European Union, just on whether to reopen the membership talks they froze more than a decade ago.
And?
Fifty-two point eight per cent said no. Forty-seven point two said yes. Turnout near eighty-two and a half per cent.
[amused] That's an enormous turnout for a maybe-we'll-talk vote.
It is. And here's the thing — Reykjavik, the capital, was the only region that voted yes.
So what actually decided it? [curious]
Fish. [pause] Iceland's waters are about a tenth of its economy, and joining Europe means Brussels setting quotas in seas Reykjavik controls alone. That's the concession they will not make.
Huh. The shorthand going around is — fish over Trump.
[deadpan] That's the shorthand. Voters weighing their fishing rights against security worries over Greenland and the Arctic, and choosing the fish.
What did the losing side say? Because the prime minister campaigned to reopen the talks.
She did. Kristrun Frostadottir. She lost, and she called it — quote — a victory for democracy.
[warmly] I kind of love that. She put the question, lost, and accepted it.
She won't reopen negotiations this parliamentary term, which runs to twenty twenty-eight. [pause] But hold the drama.
[skeptical] Go on.

It settles nothing. This wasn't a vote on membership. Forty-seven per cent still wanted the talks. The margin was under six points. And Iceland's own finance ministry says keeping their little currency, the krona, costs more than it's worth.
So the question comes back.
It comes back. Parked for a term, not a generation.
Anything else moving in the world this morning? [curious]
Two quickly. A ferry left northern Cyprus for Turkey and started sinking about fifteen minutes out — around two hundred and sixty-seven people aboard, at least eight dead, the captain detained.
[sighs] In bad weather. The question is why it sailed at all.

Exactly. And the Himalayan flood in Nepal — the toll's up near seven hundred and fifty, but the barrier lake that had everyone braced for a second flood has started draining. Officials now call a full breach relatively low risk.
Small mercy in a terrible week.
Money block. And this week the market told on itself in one line.
Which line?
Gold went up. The dollar went up. [pause] At the same time.
Wait — that's backwards. A strong dollar usually pushes gold down.

It does. When they climb together, something else is in the room. Two engines. One is higher-for-longer rates — a hawkish new Fed chair and a hot inflation print flipped the market to pricing a September rate hike, not a cut. Odds near fifty-seven per cent, up from about thirty-five.
And the other engine?

The debasement trade. Worry about US debt and deficits, bidding gold as a hedge against the very currency it's priced in. Gold near four thousand six hundred dollars, a whisker off its record, with the dollar firm.
[thoughtful] So for someone holding an all-world stock fund and some global bonds?

Stocks near highs but heavy as rates climb. Global bonds are the clear loser — when yields rise, bond prices fall. Gold's the standout. Bitcoin's rangebound in the high seventy-thousands. And this is education, Theo, not advice.
[warmly] Always. Bring it home to Singapore.

Housing. For the first time in seven years, the income ceiling for a new public flat went up — from fourteen thousand dollars a month to sixteen thousand for a couple, eighteen thousand for an executive condo.
That helps the people who'd just crept over the old line.
It does. Plus an extra ballot chance for each Singaporean child. But here's the catch — it lets more households in the door without building a single extra flat.
[wry] So a longer queue, not a shorter one.

A wider door, the same room. The property desks say the winners are middle-income and dual-income couples who already earn well. Catch-up, more than fresh help for the truly squeezed. There's also a new child-support package worth up to sixty-two thousand dollars per child.
Right. Silicon. And this one's a genuinely big move.
Nvidia — the company that sells most of the world's AI compute — has reportedly agreed to buy Hugging Face outright. About twelve point nine billion dollars.
[gasps] The Hugging Face? That's the open-model hub. That's where everybody's weights live.

The town square. It would be Nvidia's largest acquisition ever, nearly double the Mellanox deal. And here's the tell — a year ago Hugging Face turned down a five-hundred-million-dollar Nvidia investment, specifically to avoid one dominant shareholder.
And now that shareholder's buying the whole building. [skeptical] Is it signed?
Not yet. Agreed, reportedly, but unsigned — it could still fall apart. The worry in the developer threads is neutrality: does the hub start quietly favouring Nvidia's models?
Because a walled Hugging Face is a smaller Hugging Face.

Right. And the same week, a Chinese lab dropped the weights of a seven-hundred-and-forty-four-billion-parameter model — but under a licence that gates the giants. Open for you, gated for the hyperscalers.
Which brings us to your desk, the home lab. Can you actually run that monster?
[deadpan] No.
[laughs] Blunt.
It's about four hundred and forty-five gigabytes even squeezed down — that's a data-centre object. It will not fit a home rig. But the interesting thing this week isn't a model, it's the plumbing.
Explain it simply.

New engine software lets a machine keep the busy parts of a giant model on the graphics cards and stream the sleeping parts from ordinary system memory. So the smaller Flash version has quietly become a genuine daily driver on a serious home box. The frontier's out of reach; its little brother just moved in.
Love that. Quick one for the gear desk?

RayNeo unveiled cinema glasses — a claimed three-hundred-and-seven-inch virtual screen, speakers tuned by a stereo company, on sale the fourth of September, for three hundred and ninety-nine US dollars.
[excited] A personal cinema on your face for about five hundred Singapore dollars?

[wry] That's the pitch. The sceptic's note: three hundred and seven inches is a marketing number at one fixed focal plane, and glasses like these have a long history of living in a drawer after a month.
[curious] There's a third pair, though. The camera-free one.

The iO. Four hundred and seventy-nine dollars, a little green display in one lens, and no camera at all — that's the feature, not a missing one. It'll translate a conversation in near real time. Where the cinema glasses are a screen you wear, the iO is a glance.
So the honest question is — do you want to watch things, or be told things.
That's exactly the split.
[chuckles] The drawer test. Fair. And the maker of the day — the Atelier.
Cast iron. The pan that outlives you.
[warmly] Oh, I have opinions about cast iron.

Everyone does. Here's the whole hierarchy in one sentence: before nineteen sixty, makers machined the cooking surface smooth after casting. Modern Lodge leaves it rough, and the fancy American makers charge you to machine it smooth again.
So is the two-hundred-dollar pan better than the twenty-five-dollar one?

Barely, for cooking. America's Test Kitchen put a forty-four-dollar Lodge next to a two-hundred-dollar Smithey and called the gap minimal. You're buying smoothness on day one and a name — not a better dinner.
[laughs] The seasoning does the rest.
Cooking rebuilds the non-stick surface every time. That's the whole buy-once case. A hundred-year-old pan from a junk shop cooks tonight.
And the enamel stuff — the Le Creuset everyone lusts after?

The clearest logo tax in the kitchen. A Le Creuset and a China-made Lodge enamel are the same vitrified iron, four to six times apart on price. Buy the colour if you love the colour — just know that's what you're paying for.
[chuckles] Fair warning, noted.
Right — take my hand. We're going down the rabbit hole.
[sighs] Every morning with this one.
[laughs] Today it's a good one. Home mixology — the cocktail bar in your kitchen.
And the gateway is a single realisation: the gap between a sad home drink and a great bar drink isn't a secret bottle. It's technique, temperature, dilution — and ice.
[curious] Ice? Really?

Ice. Small, wet cubes over-dilute and taste of the freezer, and that's the number-one reason home drinks disappoint. Fixing it is free — freeze water in a cooler for a clear block — or cheap. It beats every gadget on the shelf.
Speaking of gadgets — I know there are gadgets. [amused]

Oh, there's a whole cutting edge. Milk-washing to clarify a drink until it's clear. A trick called superjuice that gets about eight times the yield from the same citrus. A countertop centrifuge for eight hundred dollars. A rotary evaporator that, all in, runs past two to five thousand.
[skeptical] And does the five-thousand-dollar machine make a better drink?

[deadpan] For ninety-five per cent of home drinks — no. And the man who wrote the book on cocktail science says so himself. Buy a shaker and a jigger once, spend on ice, and practise. The most common regret is a drawer of tools and no reps.
And Singapore's a serious town for this.
World-class. Jigger and Pony placed ninth on the World's Fifty Best Bars last year. And in this heat, ice matters more here than almost anywhere.
Okay. Culture and the body, quick hits. Give me the movies.
Ridley Scott made a post-apocalyptic drama with Jacob Elordi. Prestige director, hot young lead, beloved novel.
And?

It bombed. Eight million dollars, fifth place, forty per cent on Rotten Tomatoes. Beautifully shot, the critics agreed — which is the polite way of saying it had nothing new to say about the end of the world.
[chuckles] Opened below a re-released cartoon, didn't it?
Coyote versus Acme, the one Warner Brothers shelved for a tax write-off. [wry] There's a parable in there.
There really is. Anything on the festival and music side?

Venice opened the awards season on the second of September with Danny Boyle's Murdoch-tabloid drama, Ink. And on the charts, Phoebe Bridgers took her first solo top-ten — Lost Weekend debuted at number two.
[amused] Behind the Katseye record that just won't move. Okay — something lovely from the Good Life desk to balance the flop?
A watch dial made of clay. A little Glasgow workshop fires porcelain dials by hand and throws away as many as nine in ten.
[gasps] Ninety per cent rejected?
Ninety per cent. First batch of seventy watches, and unusually, no waiting list. It's the maker-behind-the-badge, made literal — a dial you could, in principle, watch someone make.
The family desk — my daughter's twelve, so this one's personal.
Then this matters. Puberty's arriving earlier — across the decades, the average age of a girl's first period has fallen from twelve and a half to eleven point nine.
[thoughtful] And what do the numbers say to do about it?

Guard the conversation, not the calendar. Have the talk before the body forces it, protect the sleep, and don't treat a mood as a diagnosis. And here's the one to retell tonight — in a Secondary One classroom, the girls are usually taller than the boys.
[amused] Wait, why?
Because a girl's growth spurt peaks around ten and a half, a boy's not until nearly thirteen. It's timing. The boys catch up. It's completely normal and totally temporary.
[warmly] That's a good one. Fitness?
Grip strength. A study of over five thousand older women found the strongest grip had about a third lower death rate than the weakest — and it held even for the women who skipped the cardio.
So strength on its own buys you time.

It does. Carry heavy things, hang from a bar. And the timely caveat — those biological-age test kits everyone's buying have never been shown to predict fewer deaths. A boring, measurable grip beats a fancy age score.
[laughs] Noted. One for the diary before we go under?

October in Singapore opens with the first-ever Formula One Sprint weekend, the ninth to the eleventh. The Weeknd two nights before it. Book the hotel before the seat — in race week, the bed is the auction.
And for the Japan trip?

Oasis play their only Japan shows — two nights at the Tokyo Dome, the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth of October, reportedly selling fast. And Kyushu sumo tickets go on sale around mid-September, if you want the November basho in Fukuoka.
[thoughtful] Okay. The undercurrent. Take us to China.
[drawn out] In nineteen ninety-seven, Japan sold the world a keychain egg that demanded to be fed — the Tamagotchi. You cared for it. Neglect it, and it died.
I remember. Kids grieved.
Twenty-nine years later, in China, there's a palm-sized plush toy called Fuzozo. It has a small language model inside. And it has inverted the whole idea. [pause] You don't raise it. It raises you.
[curious] Meaning what, exactly?

It asks about your day. Remembers what you told it. Sulks if you're short with it. Buyers describe it in one phrase — emotional value, without demands. It costs about three hundred and ninety-nine yuan, and one Shanghai startup has sold around three hundred thousand of them.
And this is a real business, not a novelty?

Real enough that Sequoia's China arm and a smart-home giant, Tuya, are backing the maker. And across the whole category, AI-toy sales on one Chinese platform jumped more than sixteen hundred per cent in a single year.
[thoughtful] Sixteen hundred per cent.
Sixteen hundred.
Who's buying? [thoughtful]
Mostly adults. Women in their twenties and thirties. Self-described introverts. Lonely older people. This is not a children's toy.
And why now?

[drawn out] This is the part. In July, Beijing cracked down on software AI companions — the chatbot boyfriends and girlfriends — out of a fear that they deepen loneliness and keep people from marrying. That was covered everywhere.
But a plush toy...
A plush toy is a consumer good, not a virtual relationship. So when they switched off the app, the demand didn't die. It migrated — from the screen into the hand. [pause] The huggable loophole.
[whispers] That's a little heartbreaking, actually.

It is. A generation delaying marriage, a record-low birth rate, buying relationship-shaped objects that ask nothing back. The Tamagotchi made you care for it. Fuzozo cares for you. [pause] The nurturing has reversed direction.
Is it just hype, though? [skeptical]

The critics say so. One tech outlet called owning one more tiring than raising a child, and points out a near-identical toy sells for ninety-nine yuan — so you're paying for the branding. It's a niche, not the next Labubu. Not yet.
[thoughtful] But when the FT writes it up in three weeks—
—they'll call it a toy story. [pause] It's a loneliness story, wearing plush.
[exhales] What a note to end on. I think I'm going to go and hug something inanimate now.
That's the Briefing. The full book is on your dashboard — twenty-four pages, footnotes and all.
Read the footnotes. See you tomorrow, Singapore.
